title: API Gateway Fundamentals
summary: What a gateway does at the edge of your system — and why that's more than "just a load balancer with extra steps."

slides.markdown:
An **API gateway** is the single front door for external traffic entering your system — it authenticates, rate-limits, routes, and transforms requests before they reach any backend service.

- It sits at the **edge**: north-south traffic, client to system.
- It centralizes cross-cutting concerns so backend services don't each reimplement auth and rate limiting.
- It's a distinct layer from a plain load balancer — routing is only one of its jobs.

slides.subTitle: Routing, auth, rate limiting, transformation
slides.markdown:
A gateway handles four core jobs before a request ever touches your backend code: **routing** (which service handles `/orders` vs `/users`), **auth termination** (verify the token once, at the edge), **rate limiting** (protect backends from being overwhelmed, per client or globally), and **transformation** (reshape a request/response — e.g. combine two backend calls into one client-facing response).

Each of these is a concern every service would otherwise have to implement itself — the gateway exists so they don't have to.

slides.subTitle: One more layer of "what," not just "where"
slides.markdown:
| | Load balancer | API gateway |
|---|---|---|
| Core question answered | Which healthy backend instance? | Which service, and is this request even allowed through? |
| Auth | Not its job | Verifies tokens/API keys |
| Rate limiting | Not its job | Per-client, per-route limits |
| Request shape | Passes through unchanged | Can transform, aggregate, version |

A load balancer answers **"where"** (which instance); a gateway answers **"what"** — is this request valid, allowed, and shaped correctly — often sitting in front of one or more load balancers, not replacing them.

slides.subTitle: The gateway's job is at the system's edge
slides.markdown:
**North-south traffic** is traffic entering or leaving your system from the outside world — a mobile app calling your API, a browser hitting your site. This is exactly where a gateway lives: it's the **single, controlled entry point** for everything external.

Traffic *between* your own internal services (**east-west**) is a different problem with different tools — that's the domain of a **service mesh**, not the gateway. Conflating the two leads to putting mesh-shaped concerns (like service-to-service mTLS) into the gateway, where they don't belong.

Real gateways vary in deployment model but share the same job: **Kong** and **NGINX** (as a gateway) are self-hosted, plugin-extensible proxies you run yourself; **cloud-managed gateways** (API Gateway-style products from major clouds) trade some flexibility for zero infrastructure to operate.

The choice is usually about **control vs operational burden** — a self-hosted gateway gives you full plugin control and no vendor lock-in; a managed one gets you running in an afternoon but couples you to that provider's feature set and limits.

slides.subTitle: Through a gateway to a backend service
slides.markdown:
![A request's path through a gateway to a backend service](assets/gateway-request-path.svg)

The client only ever talks to the gateway. The gateway authenticates and rate-limits once, then routes to whichever backend actually owns that path — the backend never has to parse a raw client token or worry about being hit directly from the open internet.

assets.alt: A request's path through a gateway to a backend service

slides.subTitle: Centralizing auth so services don't reimplement it
slides.markdown:
Without a gateway, each of 12 backend services independently validates JWTs, checks scopes, and handles expired-token errors — 12 near-identical, slightly-diverging implementations, each a place a security bug can hide.

With a gateway terminating auth: the gateway validates the token once, attaches a verified identity (e.g. a header like `X-User-Id`) to the forwarded request, and every backend just **trusts the gateway's header** instead of re-implementing token validation. One place to patch a vulnerability, one place to audit.

slides.subTitle: Business logic in the gateway layer
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to add business rules to the gateway since it already sees every request — e.g. "if this user's plan is Premium, route to the faster cluster." This creeps into **business logic living outside the service that owns the domain**, making it invisible to the team that actually understands the rule and untestable alongside that service's own logic.

Keep the gateway to cross-cutting, infrastructure-shaped concerns (auth, rate limits, routing, transformation) and leave domain decisions to the services that own that domain.

slides.sectionTitle: The gateway as a single point of failure
slides.subTitle: Why HA design matters more here than almost anywhere else
slides.markdown:
Since every external request passes through the gateway, an outage there takes down the entire system's front door — even if every backend service is perfectly healthy behind it. This makes gateway availability a uniquely high-leverage concern: a bug in one backend service degrades one feature, but a gateway crash or misconfigured deploy degrades everything at once.

In practice this means running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer (never a single gateway node), rolling out gateway config changes with the same rollout discipline as any production service (canary the routing rule, not just the code), and treating gateway capacity planning as protecting the whole system's availability, not just one component's.
